sections.body_md:
A line search has to do more than make the objective smaller. Sufficient decrease, the Armijo inequality, says the drop is at least a fraction of the drop the linear model predicted. The fraction \(c_1\) sits strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). That test can accept a step whose slope is still steeply negative, or even a step whose slope has become more negative. Later updates that divide by the curvature of the gradient need something stronger.

The curvature test looks at the directional derivative at the new point. It asks that new derivative to be at least \(c_2\) times the old one, with \(c_1 < c_2 < 1\). The old directional derivative of a descent direction is negative, so \(c_2\) times it is less negative. The slope along the step has to rise at least that far, and it does not have to reach zero.

Together the two inequalities force a positive curvature product. Let \(s\) be the step and let \(y\) be the change in the gradient. Curvature says the new directional derivative is at least \(c_2\) times the old one. Subtract the old derivative, multiply by the positive length, and the product \(y^T s\) is bounded below by a positive number. The gap \(c_2 < 1\) and the negative old derivative are what make the lower bound positive. Sufficient decrease alone does not.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(0 < c_1 < c_2 < 1\),
\[
f(x+td) \le f(x) + c_1 t \nabla f(x)^T d,
\]
\[
\nabla f(x+td)^T d \ge c_2 \nabla f(x)^T d.
\]
Writing \(s = t d\) and \(y\) for the gradient change, these force \(y^T s > 0\) when the old directional derivative is negative.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(f(t) = 4t^2\), so the derivative is \(8t\). Start at \(t = 3\) and step in the direction \(d = -1\) with length \(1\). The old derivative is \(24\). The new point is \(2\), where the derivative is \(16\). The step \(s\) equals \(-1\), and the gradient change \(y\) equals \(16 - 24\).

The hawser product is 8. The product \(y s\) is positive. A decrease test would also have passed, because the value falls from \(36\) to \(16\). The product, not the decrease, is the quantity a curvature-sensitive update needs. On a function that bends the other way, a decrease test can pass while this product is negative.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Checking curvature with the opposite inequality accepts steps whose slope became steeper. That is the case the test is written to reject. A second slip is to set \(c_2\) below \(c_1\), or to set \(c_2\) at least \(1\). The positive-product argument uses the strict gap between them. A third is to treat a negative curvature product as harmless because the objective fell. An update that divides by that product, or that expects a positive definite Hessian approximation, cannot use the step. A fourth is to require the new directional derivative to be zero. That is an exact line search. Wolfe is weaker, and the weaker test is enough for the sign of \(y^T s\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The positive product is the hypothesis a BFGS update uses to stay positive definite. A line search that stops at sufficient decrease can return a step whose product is negative, and the update built from that step can lose positive definiteness. Asking for both Wolfe tests before the update is what keeps the curvature hypothesis available.
